strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer-vision problem: accelerating high-resolution diffusion generation without retraining while preserving perceptual quality. Using aesthetic-token affinity to allocate spatial computation is a plausible contribution under Algorithms/General.

The reported Lumina results are promising: latency decreases from 12.37 s to 5.86 s, while ImageReward increases from 0.7518 to 0.8410. The component ablations show benefits from combining spatial computation reduction and temporal reuse, and Table 8 supports aesthetic-aware token weighting over uniform and non-aesthetic alternatives.

The evaluation reports 10,000 prompts with three paired seeds, several preference and alignment metrics, and comparisons with relevant acceleration methods. The appendix provides useful anchor vocabulary, hardware settings, sensitivity studies, and architecture-specific limitations.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the claimed cross-backbone generality of aesthetic spatial allocation. Appendix A.3 states that SD3 retains temporal StepCache without region-wise CFG, while FLUX mainly uses temporal reuse because the spatial path is unsupported. Nevertheless, Sections 4.2–4.4 and Figure 6 attribute SD3 improvements to preserving aesthetically salient updates and reallocating spatial guidance. These results establish broader applicability of caching, but do not validate the central aesthetic mechanism across three architectures. The executed components must be specified unambiguously and the claims narrowed accordingly.

The ablations do not separate spatial guidance from spatial computation reduction. Stronger foreground CFG could explain much of the quality improvement attributed to selective computation. A dense model with the same spatial CFG, sparse computation with uniform CFG, and appropriately tuned dense guidance are needed to establish the proposed coupling's benefit. Moreover, the motivating claim that aesthetic-affinity regions exhibit greater temporal variation or extrapolation error is asserted without quantitative trajectory analysis. This leaves the scientific distinction from existing region-adaptive sampling and forecasting methods insufficiently established.

Several central algorithm details are inconsistent or underspecified. Equations 12–13 call tau the latest evaluated timestep, yet use a prediction at tau+Delta to estimate t between those endpoints; neither increasing-step nor decreasing-diffusion-time indexing makes the stated interval and extrapolation convention consistent. Section 3.2 selects top-r tokens without specifying r, whereas the appendix describes threshold-based anchor weighting. Also, uniformly aggregating all text-token attention under Equation 2's normalization produces a constant spatial map, so the nonuniform uniform-token fallback requires an additional rule. These issues need executable pseudocode, not merely descriptive clarification.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the appendix. The foreground/background guidance scales, precise background-activation refresh schedule, and mapping between CLIP tokens and each backbone's conditioning tokens are not specified. It is also unclear when a 'full forward' refreshes all spatial activations versus executing the sparse path. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no usable link. These omissions affect reproduction of both quality gains and runtime.

The evaluation distribution favors the proposed aesthetic prior, and its construction is insufficiently documented. Appendix E identifies the main subset as aesthetics-oriented, with a 65.48% anchor-trigger rate versus 44.9% in the complete unique prompt pool. Results on an unselected sample and separate triggered/non-triggered subsets would clarify generalization. No confidence intervals or human preference study are provided; these are particularly relevant to the smaller improvements and the broad aesthetic-quality claims. Edge density alone cannot distinguish desirable detail from artifacts.

The speed–quality comparisons use isolated default operating points rather than matched-latency or matched-quality sweeps, and omit a simple reduced-step sampling baseline. On FLUX, TaylorSeer is faster (5.96 s versus 7.31 s), has slightly higher HPS, and nearly matches ImageReward, so the evidence supports a trade-off rather than broad superiority. Reporting approximately identical 2.11× speedup across skip ratios 0.30–0.70 also needs more precise profiling, since spatial sparsification alone reportedly saves 29.5% of runtime.

There are reporting inconsistencies that should be corrected: Lumina's full-method aesthetic score is 6.1414 in Table 1 and 6.141 in Table 7, but 6.041 in Table 2. Figure 5's spatial-only speedup and ImageReward also mix values associated with different spatial variants in Table 7. These may be editorial errors, but they obscure which configuration supports the reported improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer-vision problem: reducing high-resolution diffusion-transformer inference cost without retraining. Using prompt-conditioned attention to prioritize spatial computation is a plausible contribution under Algorithms/General.

The reported Lumina results are promising: latency decreases from 12.37 to 5.86 seconds while ImageReward increases from 0.752 to 0.841. Table 7 separates spatial and temporal components, and Table 8 reports an additional benefit from aesthetic-aware token selection over uniform weighting.

The evaluation reports 10,000 prompts with three paired seeds, multiple quality proxies, three backbones, and end-to-end timing. The appendix provides useful anchor lists, hardware details, sensitivity experiments, and explicit architectural limitations.
weaknesses: The claimed cross-backbone validation of aesthetic spatial allocation is not supported by the implemented configurations. Appendix A.3 states that SD3 retains temporal StepCache without region-wise CFG, while FLUX mainly uses temporal reuse because the spatial path is unsupported. Nevertheless, Sections 4.2–4.4 and Figure 6 attribute these results to preserving aesthetic regions and reallocating spatial computation and guidance. Temporal-only improvements cannot establish transfer of the central spatial mechanism.

The ablations do not isolate aesthetic compute allocation from guidance changes. The spatial path also changes CFG, but there is no dense-computation baseline with the same spatial guidance, nor a clear sparse-computation comparison with guidance held fixed. Consequently, the quality gains cannot confidently be attributed to selective computation. The motivating claim that aesthetic-affinity regions have greater temporal variation and extrapolation error is also asserted without quantitative trajectory analysis.

AesMask is not specified consistently enough to reproduce. Section 3.2 selects top-r tokens, whereas the appendix describes threshold-based anchor weighting and a fallback, without explaining their relationship or specifying r. More fundamentally, uniform weighting over all text tokens in the row-normalized attention of Equation 2 produces a spatially constant sum. The nonuniform uniform-weighting heatmap and fallback therefore require an undocumented token exclusion, normalization, or aggregation rule.

The temporal predictor has an indexing/sign ambiguity. Equations 12–13 call tau the latest evaluated timestep, retain E_(tau+Delta), and predict at t in (tau, tau+Delta). With descending diffusion time, that interval lies behind the latest evaluation; with ascending time, the second cached output would be unavailable. An explicit causal schedule and consistent extrapolation formula are needed. The spatial background-cache refresh schedule and numerical CFG scales are also insufficiently documented.

Comparative evidence is limited to selected operating points, with competing methods using official/default intervals. Matched-latency or matched-quality sweeps and a reduced-step dense sampler would better establish the advantage over simpler acceleration. This matters on FLUX: TaylorSeer is faster (2.12× versus 1.73×), has slightly higher HPS, and nearly matches ImageReward. The results support a trade-off rather than broad superiority.

The evaluation subset favors the proposed semantic prior: Appendix E reports anchor activation on 65.48% of evaluation prompts versus 44.9% of the full unique prompt pool. The selection procedure and separate results on triggered/non-triggered prompts are missing. Automated preference scores provide useful evidence, but without uncertainty estimates or human preference evaluation, small gains and broad aesthetic-improvement claims remain insufficiently established.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence but are individually correctable: Lumina Aesthetic score is 6.1414 in Table 1 versus 6.041 in Table 2; the stated approximately 46% theoretical skip rate is not reconciled with five warmup steps and alternate-step reuse; and Table 9 reports essentially identical speedups across substantially different spatial sparsities despite a sizable standalone spatial speedup. These discrepancies should be resolved with precise schedules and measured timings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: accelerating high-resolution DiT inference while preserving perceptually important regions. Using prompt-conditioned aesthetic affinity to allocate computation is a plausible and useful direction.

The reported Lumina results are promising: latency decreases from 12.37 to 5.86 seconds, while ImageReward increases from 0.7518 to 0.8410. Evaluation uses 10,000 prompts with three paired seeds, multiple quality metrics, and several relevant acceleration baselines.

The component ablations provide useful evidence of complementary spatial and temporal acceleration. Table 8 also supports an incremental benefit from aesthetic weighting over uniform token weighting. The appendix documents hardware, anchor vocabulary, mask timing, and several sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The claimed generality of aesthetic spatial allocation is not established. Appendix A.3 states that FLUX mainly uses StepCache and describes SD3 as retaining temporal caching without region-wise CFG; their standalone StepCache speedups exactly match the full-method speedups. Nevertheless, Sections 4.2–4.4 and Figure 6 attribute these results to aesthetic spatial allocation and, for SD3, spatial guidance. The precise active components must be specified, and temporal-only results cannot validate the central aesthetic mechanism across architectures.

The experiments do not adequately separate aesthetic compute allocation from guidance changes. Spatial CFG modifies the generation objective, but its numerical scales are unspecified, and there is no dense-plus-spatial-CFG control or clear sparse-computation ablation with guidance held fixed. Consequently, the substantial quality improvement cannot confidently be attributed to preserving aesthetically important computation. The stated observation that high-affinity regions vary more temporally also lacks quantitative validation.

Core implementation details are inconsistent or incomplete. Section 3.2 selects top-r prompt tokens, whereas the appendix describes thresholded anchor weighting and a uniform-weight fallback, without defining their relationship or r. Under Equation 2's normalization, uniformly summing attention over all text tokens gives a constant spatial map, so the nontrivial uniform/fallback heatmaps require additional explanation. Background activation refresh and the mapping between CLIP tokens and backbone text tokens are also insufficiently specified.

The StepCache equations do not clearly define an executable causal extrapolation scheme. Equations 12–13 use predictions at tau and tau+Delta for t between them; with increasing indices, one endpoint is not yet available, while decreasing diffusion time does not resolve the stated interval and extrapolation direction. This may be a notation error, but explicit sampling-order pseudocode is needed because this component provides most of the demonstrated acceleration.

Baseline comparisons use official/default settings rather than matched-latency tuning or speed–quality curves, and omit a straightforward reduced-step sampler control. This limits the claimed superiority over forecasting and caching methods. On FLUX, for example, TaylorSeer is faster (5.96 versus 7.31 seconds), has slightly higher HPS, and nearly matches ImageReward. The missing comparisons matter particularly because FLUX primarily evaluates temporal reuse.

The evaluation supports narrower conclusions than the broad aesthetic-enhancement claims. The evaluation subset is enriched for anchor-triggering prompts (65.48% versus 44.9% in the source pool), but its selection procedure and separate triggered/non-triggered results are not provided. There are no uncertainty estimates or direct human preference measurements, and edge density is not intrinsically a quality measure. Reporting inconsistencies also need correction: Lumina's full-method aesthetic score is 6.1414 in Table 1 but 6.041 in Table 2. Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet overcome the methodological and attribution concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: accelerating high-resolution text-to-image generation while preserving perceptual quality. Using prompt-conditioned aesthetic affinity to allocate spatial computation is a plausible contribution under Algorithms/General.

The reported Lumina results are promising: latency decreases from 12.37 s to 5.86 s while ImageReward increases from 0.752 to 0.841. Tables 8 and 12 provide useful evidence that spatial sparsification and temporal reuse contribute complementary benefits.

The evaluation includes three backbones, multiple quality metrics, paired prompts and seeds, and end-to-end latency. Comparisons include relevant spatial methods such as RAS and SDiT, alongside temporal caching methods.

The human preference study provides evidence beyond automatic reward metrics, reporting 67% preference over dense generation. Descriptor-free prompts, complex scenes, static-versus-dynamic masks, and failure analysis broaden the evaluation and acknowledge meaningful limitations.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central aesthetic-allocation contribution from guidance changes. Lumina simultaneously changes spatial computation and CFG, but there is no quantitative quality comparison against dense inference with the same Spatial-CFG, or against suitably tuned uniform CFG. Table 16 reports only latency for the dense-compute guidance variant. The human comparison against a variant without Spatial-CFG reinforces that guidance matters but does not separate its benefit from sparsification. Meanwhile, removing AesMask retains most of the ImageReward improvement (0.822 versus 0.841, from a 0.752 baseline).

Essential implementation details are missing despite the extensive appendix. Table 4 never specifies the numerical value of top-r; the guidance scales are unspecified; and mapping CLIP token similarities to each backbone's conditioning tokens is unclear. Background attention outputs, cache refresh rules for background activations, and extracting attention from SD3's joint attention are insufficiently described. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no link. These omissions materially impede reproduction.

The temporal-cache specification contains unresolved inconsistencies. Equations 12–13 identify the latest evaluated timestep as τ but use an interval and extrapolation sign that do not consistently describe causal prediction from two previous evaluations. Table 5's roughly 46% skipped-step fractions also do not follow straightforwardly from five initial full steps and alternating evaluations over 28–30 steps. The four-step FLUX-schnell result needs a separate configuration because the stated five-step warmup and mask construction would not activate. Explicit sampling pseudocode and per-backbone schedules are needed.

The cross-backbone interpretation exceeds the evidence. Appendix A.3 states that FLUX primarily uses StepCache because the spatial path is unsupported; its results therefore do not validate aesthetic spatial allocation, contrary to the interpretation in Sections 4.2–4.3. SD3 lacks a component ablation, and its standalone StepCache speedup already equals the reported full-method speedup. The complete proposed mechanism is convincingly exercised only on Lumina.

The claimed speed–quality frontier is not established by single operating points. Baseline hyperparameters and tuning budgets are not reported, FORA provides essentially no acceleration on Lumina or SD3, and reduced-step dense sampling is absent. On FLUX, TaylorSeer is substantially faster with similar preference scores. Matched-latency comparisons or parameter sweeps are necessary to distinguish a superior allocation strategy from different operating-point choices.

The central mechanistic observation—that aesthetic-affinity regions vary more temporally and are harder to extrapolate—is illustrated indirectly through heatmaps rather than measured through regional temporal variation or prediction errors. Generic semantic/saliency controls would also help distinguish aesthetic specificity from ordinary subject selection. Statistical reporting leaves additional uncertainty: automatic metrics lack confidence intervals, the aesthetics-enriched 10,000-prompt subset has no reproducible selection rule or separate tuning split, and the human study omits tie counts and allocation across comparisons. Its binomial significance analysis does not explain how repeated judgments of the same pairs are handled.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer-vision problem: accelerating high-resolution diffusion transformers while preserving perceptual quality. Using prompt-conditioned aesthetic affinity to allocate computation is a plausible contribution under Algorithms/General.

The reported Lumina results are promising: latency decreases from 12.37 s to 5.86 s, while ImageReward increases from 0.752 to 0.841. Evaluation includes several preference and alignment metrics, 10,000 prompts with three seeds, and end-to-end timing.

The component ablations provide useful evidence of complementarity. StepCache alone slightly reduces ImageReward, whereas the spatial path improves it; anchor-aware masking also outperforms uniform and non-aesthetic token weighting (Tables 8–9).

The authors supplement automatic scores with a blinded human study, descriptor-free prompts, complex scenes, mask-refresh experiments, and discussion of failure cases. These are meaningful efforts to assess practical limitations.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently established. The paper asserts that aesthetic-affinity regions exhibit greater temporal variation and are harder to extrapolate, but provides no quantitative relationship between affinity, temporal prediction error, and the benefit of preserving computation. Attention visualizations and aggregate quality improvements do not establish this explanation.

Quality improvements are not adequately separated from changes in guidance. Spatial CFG changes the sampling objective alongside computational sparsification. Although the human study compares against a variant without Spatial CFG, there is no complete quantitative control using dense computation with identical spatial guidance, or an equivalently tuned global-guidance baseline. Table 16 reports only the latency of the dense-compute guidance configuration. Consequently, the evidence does not isolate how much improvement comes from aesthetic compute allocation.

Cross-backbone claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Appendix A.3 states that FLUX mainly uses temporal StepCache and does not expose the proposed spatial SkipSparse path; its results therefore do not validate aesthetic spatial allocation. SD3 disables spatial CFG. Furthermore, Table 7 shows TaylorSeer is faster on FLUX (2.12× versus 1.73×) with nearly identical ImageReward (1.304 versus 1.317) and slightly higher HPS, making the claimed superiority less clear without matched-latency comparisons.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Table 4 never specifies the numerical top-r selection setting, and the spatial guidance scales, background-cache refresh schedule, and mapping between CLIP tokens and backbone conditioning tokens are not sufficiently described. Equations 12–13 also give an inconsistent extrapolation interval: with decreasing diffusion time, the next prediction should lie below the latest evaluated timestep, not between that timestep and the previous one. This may be a notation error, but no executable pseudocode or working code link resolves it.

Baseline calibration is insufficiently documented. The paper reports isolated operating points without cache thresholds, refresh configurations, or speed–quality sweeps. FORA obtains essentially no acceleration while substantially reducing quality, which warrants implementation diagnostics. Comparisons against reduced-step sampling and existing accelerators equipped with the same guidance would better establish the incremental value over known caching, regional allocation, and guidance techniques.

Generalization and statistical evidence have important limits. Appendix F identifies the evaluation subset as aesthetics-oriented, with anchor hits in 65.48% of prompts versus 44.9% in the source pool, but does not explain its selection reproducibly. The human study does not clearly report pair allocation across comparisons, tie counts, or uncertainty accounting for repeated ratings of the same images. The four-step FLUX-schnell result also lacks an explanation of how the default five-step warmup and mask construction were adapted. These gaps prevent the additional experiments from fully resolving the main concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer vision problem: accelerating high-resolution diffusion generation while preserving perceptually important regions. Combining prompt-conditioned spatial allocation, spatial guidance, and temporal reuse is a useful training-free design.

The reported Lumina results are compelling: latency decreases from 12.37 s to 5.86 s while ImageReward increases from 0.752 to 0.841, with improvements in CLIP, HPS, and aesthetic scores. Evaluating 10,000 prompts with three shared seeds provides substantial paired experimental coverage.

The ablations provide evidence for complementary components. StepCache alone delivers 1.57× acceleration, spatial computation alone delivers 1.43×, and aesthetic-aware token weighting improves ImageReward from 0.8222 to 0.8410 over uniform weighting.

The human preference study supports perceptible improvements beyond automated reward scores, reporting 67% overall preference and 68% visual-appeal preference against dense inference. Descriptor-free prompts, complex scenes, static-mask comparisons, and overhead measurements provide useful additional validation.
The appendix acknowledges architectural restrictions and early-mask failure cases. These disclosures help identify the method’s practical scope.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly separate better guidance from better computation allocation. Lumina changes spatial CFG as well as sparsity, but numerical guidance scales are omitted, and the dense-compute AesMask + Spatial-CFG control reports latency without quality metrics (Table 16). The human comparison against the variant without spatial CFG actually suggests guidance contributes substantially. Quality comparisons using the same guidance for dense inference and competing accelerators are needed to establish the claimed acceleration advantage.

The central aesthetics-aware mechanism is not validated across all three advertised backbones. Appendix A.3 states that FLUX mainly uses temporal StepCache without the spatial SkipSparse path, while SD3 disables spatial CFG. Thus FLUX improvements cannot establish transfer of aesthetic spatial allocation, despite stronger interpretations in the main text. Moreover, Table 7 shows TaylorSeer is faster (2.12× versus 1.73×), with very similar ImageReward and slightly higher HPS; the trade-off is more qualified than the broad superiority claims suggest.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Table 4 specifies 'top-r' without giving r; spatial guidance scales, background-activation refresh scheduling, and text-token alignment across encoders are insufficiently specified. Equations 12–13 also mix a latest descending diffusion timestep with an intermediate interval above that timestep, leaving the causal extrapolation order and sign unclear. Explicit sampling pseudocode is needed. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no link.

Baseline comparisons use single operating points without sufficient reproduction settings or matched-latency parameter sweeps. FORA provides effectively no acceleration while substantially reducing quality, and several other baselines suffer large reward drops. These results warrant implementation diagnostics before concluding that the proposed method establishes a better speed–quality frontier. A reduced-step dense sampler is also an important missing control for the temporal-skipping component.

The main evaluation subset is enriched for the proposed semantic prior: Appendix F reports anchor-hit rates of 65.48% in the selected 10,000 prompts versus 44.9% in the full prompt pool. The selection procedure and separation of tuning from evaluation are unclear. The 200-prompt descriptor experiment is helpful but does not establish performance on a representative unfiltered distribution. Likewise, qualitative attention maps do not directly verify the claimed relationship between aesthetic affinity and temporal prediction error.

Uncertainty reporting is inadequate for several claims. Automatic metrics have no paired confidence intervals, and the human study does not clearly describe allocation of its 60 pairs across comparisons, tie counts, or treatment of repeated judgments from the same annotators and image pairs. A simple binomial test does not address that dependence. Overall, the promising empirical results are outweighed slightly by unresolved attribution, reproducibility, and comparison concerns.
